title: A code that was literally cracked
text: DNA and RNA store instructions in a four-letter alphabet. After George Gamow proposed a number-based scheme in 1954, Crick and colleagues showed in 1961 that the code is read in triplets. In the same year Nirenberg and Matthaei fed cells' protein machinery an artificial RNA of only U and obtained a chain of phenylalanine: a known-plaintext attack on life's code, with UUU as the first entry in the table.

title: A homophonic code
text: Sixty-four codons encode 20 amino acids and stop signals, so most amino acids have several codons. That is the same structure as a homophonic cipher, in which one plaintext letter has several ciphertext symbols. Biology uses the slack differently: the choice among synonymous codons can affect how fast proteins are made.

title: Built-in damage limitation
text: Similar codons tend to encode similar amino acids, so a single-letter mutation often does little harm. Freeland and Hurst estimated in 1998 that the standard code outperforms roughly one in a million random codes at this. Crick's wobble hypothesis explains why the third position can often vary.

title: Proofreading
text: Copying enzymes check their work and repair crews fix mismatches, cutting error rates by orders of magnitude. Double-stranded DNA holds a complementary backup, a form of redundancy that engineers would recognise. The Error correction pages in Theory show the engineered versions, from parity bits to Reed-Solomon.

title: CRISPR: a record of past attackers
text: Bacteria store snippets of viral DNA in their own genome and use them to recognise and cut future invaders. Barrangou and colleagues showed in 2007 that this adds acquired immunity: a heritable database of attack signatures.

title: Calcium: information in frequency
text: Cells can encode messages in the timing of calcium signals as well as in their size. Dolmetsch and colleagues showed in 1998 that oscillation frequency changes which genes are switched on, and De Koninck and Schulman showed the same year that the enzyme CaMKII can decode oscillation frequency. It is frequency modulation in living cells.

title: Neural codes
text: Neurons send all-or-nothing spikes. Information can lie in their rate, precise timing or the pattern across a population, and how the brain uses each of these remains an active research question.

title: Quorum sensing
text: Bacteria release signal molecules and act only when the concentration shows that enough neighbours are present. The bioluminescent Vibrio fischeri lights up only at high density, in effect taking a chemical vote.

title: The honeybee dance
text: A returning forager waggles at an angle from vertical that matches the food's direction relative to the sun, and its waggle duration indicates distance. Karl von Frisch decoded this, and shared the 1973 Nobel Prize.

title: Private channels
text: Mantis shrimps can detect circularly polarised light, which Chiou and colleagues reported in 2008 and which may serve as a signalling channel few other animals can perceive. Some signals are effectively encrypted by the receiver's senses.

title: Forged messages
text: Female Photuris fireflies imitate the flash replies of other species to lure males and eat them. In cryptographic terms, it is spoofing an authentication signal.

title: A split message
text: Male mourning cuttlefish have been seen displaying male courtship patterns to a female on one side of the body while showing female patterns on the side facing a rival, as Brown and colleagues described in 2012. Two audiences get two messages at once.

title: Camouflage and mimicry
text: Camouflage is natural steganography: it hides the fact that a signal, the animal, is there at all. Harmless species that mimic dangerous ones are forging a warning signal, and they rely on predators being unable to check it.

title: Messages hidden in DNA
text: In 1999 Clelland, Risca and Bancroft hid a message in DNA among a large excess of random strands: steganography using molecules. Later work by Church and colleagues in 2012 and Goldman and colleagues in 2013 stored whole books and files in synthetic DNA.

title: A song is a sequence of symbols
text: Many songbirds sing distinct syllables in ordered phrases, and the order is not random. Bengalese finch song follows probabilistic rules that are often modelled as a Markov chain, so the same tools used on ciphers (symbol counts, entropy, which symbol follows which) describe it. The Sound Lab segments a recording into syllables, sorts them into types, and measures the sequence in bits.

title: Learned dialects
text: Song is learned from adults during a sensitive period, and young birds raised without a tutor sing abnormal songs. Peter Marler's work on white-crowned sparrows in the 1960s showed local dialects that change across short distances, much as accents do.

title: Word order in a bird call
text: Japanese tits combine an alert call with a recruitment call in a fixed order. Suzuki, Wheatcroft and Griesser reported in 2016 that birds respond appropriately to the usual order but much less to the reversed one, evidence that the order itself carries meaning.

title: Identifying the singer
text: BirdNET, a neural network from the Cornell Lab of Ornithology and Chemnitz University of Technology, names species from 3-second clips. It is very good but not a judge: on our five reference recordings it ranked the right species first every time, yet runner-up species often scored above 0.6. Treat it as a list of candidates, confirmed by the spectrogram and by where the recording was made.

title: Pheromones: messages made of molecules
text: Adolf Butenandt identified the first pheromone, bombykol from the silk moth, in 1959 after processing hundreds of thousands of moths. A male's antennae can respond to tiny amounts drifting downwind. Many moth species use blends of two or three compounds, and males respond best to their own species' ratio.
encoding: Which molecules are present and in what ratio: a species-specific key.

title: Ant trails that forget
text: Foraging ants lay trail pheromone on the way back from food, and other ants follow and reinforce it. The chemical evaporates, so trails to exhausted sources fade without anyone deciding to stop. The same idea, reinforcement plus decay, inspired ant colony optimisation algorithms in the early 1990s.
encoding: Concentration along a path, which rises with use and decays with time.

title: Plants calling for bodyguards
text: Maize attacked by caterpillars releases a blend of volatile chemicals that attracts parasitic wasps, which lay eggs in the caterpillars. Turlings, Tumlinson and Lewis reported this in 1990. The blend differs from the response to simple mechanical damage, so it carries information about the attacker.
encoding: A changed mixture of airborne compounds, triggered by chemicals in the caterpillar's saliva.

title: Bacteria that compare now with then
text: An E. coli cell cannot sense a gradient across its tiny body. Instead it swims, compares the current concentration of food with what it sensed a few seconds earlier, and tumbles less often when things are improving. The short-term memory is stored chemically, in methyl groups added to its receptors.
encoding: A difference over time, held as a chemical memory on the receptors.

title: The disputed wood wide web
text: Fungal threads connect the roots of many plants, and popular accounts describe trees warning and feeding one another through them. A 2023 review by Karst, Jones and Hoeksema found that the field evidence for these claims is much weaker than often stated. The network is real; what flows through it, and whether it carries messages, is still debated.
encoding: Unknown: this is an open question, not an established code.

title: Firefly flash codes
text: Each firefly species has its own pattern of flashes: their length, the gaps between them, and the delay before a female answers. Males and females identify each other by timing, much like Morse code. That is what lets Photuris females forge another species' reply.
encoding: Timing: flash length, interval and response delay.

title: Skin that displays patterns
text: Cuttlefish, squid and octopuses change their skin within a fraction of a second using thousands of colour-filled sacs, the chromatophores, each opened by muscles under direct nervous control. Cuttlefish can send dark bands rippling across the body, the 'passing cloud' display. Most cephalopods appear to have only one type of visual pigment, so how they match colours remains a puzzle.
encoding: Spatial patterns and moving waves across the skin, switched by nerves.

title: Warning colours as a shared standard
text: Toxic animals often advertise with bold colours, and predators learn to avoid them. When several toxic species share the same pattern, as in some Heliconius butterflies, each pays less of the cost of teaching predators. Fritz Müller described this in 1878. It is a shared standard, unlike the forged warnings of harmless mimics.
encoding: A conspicuous pattern whose meaning predators learn from experience.

title: Alarm calls that name the predator
text: Vervet monkeys give different alarm calls for leopards, eagles and snakes. In playback experiments, Seyfarth, Cheney and Marler (1980) found that monkeys hearing a recorded call responded as if to that predator, running into trees, looking up or looking down. The calls behave like words for categories.
encoding: Discrete call types, each mapped to a kind of predator.

title: Dolphins' names
text: Bottlenose dolphins develop a signature whistle with a distinctive pattern of rising and falling pitch. Janik, Sayigh and Wells reported in 2006 that dolphins respond to the whistle's contour even when the caller's voice is removed by synthesis, so the identity lies in the pattern, like a name.
encoding: The shape of a whistle's pitch over time, independent of the voice.

title: Whale song that spreads
text: Payne and McVay showed in 1971 that humpback whales sing long songs built from units, phrases and repeated themes. Garland and colleagues reported in 2011 that new songs spread eastward across South Pacific populations over several years, a cultural change moving through an ocean.
encoding: A hierarchy of units, phrases and themes, learned and copied.

title: Bat sonar and moths that jam it
text: Bats locate prey from echoes: the delay gives distance, and in horseshoe bats the Doppler shift gives relative speed, which they correct for by adjusting their call frequency. Some tiger moths fight back: Corcoran, Barber and Conner reported in 2009 that Bertholdia trigona produces ultrasonic clicks that jam bat sonar.
encoding: Echo delay for distance and frequency shift for speed; the moth's clicks add noise to the channel.

title: Messages through stems and leaves
text: Many insects, including treehoppers, communicate by vibrating the plant they stand on. These signals are nearly silent through the air, so they form a channel that predators and people easily miss. Rex Cocroft and others recorded them with laser vibrometers.
encoding: Patterns of vibration travelling through the plant.

title: Rumbles below hearing
text: Elephants make low rumbles that reach below the range of human hearing and can carry for kilometres. Caitlin O'Connell-Rodwell and colleagues have proposed that elephants also detect the vibrations these calls send through the ground, possibly through their feet.
encoding: Low frequencies, which lose less energy over distance.

title: Fish that broadcast on their own channel
text: Weakly electric fish sense their surroundings with an electric field and also communicate with it. Each discharge has a species-typical waveform and frequency. When two Eigenmannia with similar frequencies meet, each shifts its frequency away from the other's, the jamming avoidance response, much as radios keep to separate channels.
encoding: Discharge waveform and frequency, adjusted to avoid interference.

title: Maps inside the brain
text: Edgar Adrian found in the 1920s that a sensory nerve signals stronger stimuli by firing more often: a rate code. Later, John O'Keefe found place cells (1971) that fire when an animal is at a particular spot, and May-Britt and Edvard Moser found grid cells (2005) that fire on a hexagonal lattice across space. The three shared the 2014 Nobel Prize.
encoding: Firing rate for intensity; which cells fire, and when, for position.

title: Signals that are costly to fake
text: Amotz Zahavi argued in 1975 that some signals are honest because they are costly, like a peacock's tail that only a fit male can afford. Alan Grafen gave the idea a formal model in 1990, and how widely it applies is still argued. The logic resembles proof of work: a message is believable when producing it is expensive.
encoding: Cost: only a sender of high quality can afford the signal.

title: Marking your own DNA
text: Many bacteria cut foreign DNA with restriction enzymes at particular short sequences. Their own DNA carries methyl marks at those same sites, which protect it. This works like an access list: unmarked DNA, such as an invading virus's, is treated as hostile.
encoding: Chemical marks at specific sequences that distinguish self from foreign.

title: Showing the inside on the outside
text: Most cells of the body display fragments of the proteins they are making on molecules called MHC. Patrolling T cells inspect these fragments, and a cell showing foreign fragments, for example from a virus, can be destroyed. It is a continuous audit of each cell's contents.
encoding: Short protein fragments presented at the cell surface for inspection.
